concepts.name: The atom, the smallest unit of an element
concepts.why: Everything in this chapter is about the atom, so the reader should first know what the word means and how old the idea is. Democritus called the smallest unit that cannot be further subdivided the atom; we now know that atoms can be subdivided, but their identity is destroyed in the process. Atoms combine to form molecules, the smallest unit of compounds, and the fixed mass ratios of chemical reactions were the first strong, if indirect, evidence that they are there.
concepts.evidence: The book traces the idea from Leucippus and Democritus to Dalton and Avogadro, and says that the masses of reactants in specific chemical reactions always have a particular mass ratio, which is very strong indirect evidence that there are basic units that have these same mass ratios. The section summary states that atoms are the smallest unit of elements and that atoms combine to form molecules.

concepts.name: Brownian motion, the first direct evidence of atoms
concepts.why: Kinetic theory explained the gas laws so well that most scientists believed in atoms, but it was still indirect evidence. Brownian motion is the step from belief to observation: a visible particle in a fluid is struck unevenly by invisible molecules and moves first this way, then that. The reader should see that we can watch the effect of individual molecules even when the molecules themselves cannot be seen.
concepts.evidence: The book says that Robert Brown noticed in 1827 that pollen grains suspended in still water moved about in complex paths, that the motion is caused by the random thermal motions of fluid molecules colliding with the particles, and that the accurate observation and analysis of Brownian motion was the first truly direct evidence of atoms. Figure 30.2 draws the path of a pollen grain measured every few seconds.

concepts.name: Atoms are about $10^{-10}$ m across
concepts.why: Once atoms are real, the next question is how big they are, and Einstein's theory of Brownian motion answered it. Perrin's measurements gave accurate sizes of about $10^{-10}$ m, and knowing the size of an atom gives Avogadro's number, since if we know how big an atom is, we know how many fit into a certain volume. This size is the scale against which the nucleus of 30.2 turns out to be astonishingly small.
concepts.evidence: The book says that Perrin carefully observed Brownian motion, confirmed Einstein's theory and produced accurate sizes for atoms and molecules, which allowed a precise value for Avogadro's number. The section summary gives the size as $10^{-10}$ m on average, and the third conceptual question asks why atoms cannot be seen with visible light.

concepts.name: Cathode rays are streams of electrons
concepts.why: The electron was found in a glowing tube, and the reader should know what the tube showed. In a gas discharge tube, electrons freed from the gas are accelerated from the cathode to the anode, and their path is bent by a magnet in the direction expected for a negative charge. This is the apparatus Thomson turned into a measuring instrument, and it is the ancestor of the x-ray tube of 30.4.
concepts.evidence: The book says that Crookes showed that the rays carry momentum and that their normally straight path is bent by a magnet in the direction expected for a negative charge moving away from the cathode, and that these were the first direct indications of electrons and their charge. Figure 30.4 shows a gas discharge tube glowing.

concepts.name: The electron's charge-to-mass ratio, $\kqe/m_{\text{e}} = -1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg
concepts.why: Thomson could not measure the electron's charge or mass alone, but he could measure their ratio, and that ratio was enough to show that the electron is a tiny part of the atom. Crossed electric and magnetic fields select the electrons' speed, the deflection in the electric field gives their acceleration, and the ratio follows as $\kqe/m_{\text{e}} = \ka/\kEf$. The number is about a thousand times the charge per kilogram needed to plate a material, which says that the electron has a very small mass.
concepts.evidence: The book derives $q_e/m_e = a/E$ from $F = q_eE$ and $a = F/m_e$, gives the value $-1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg, and compares it with the proton's $9.58 \times 10^{7}$ C/kg, which is 1836 times less charge per kilogram. Figures 30.6 and 30.7 draw Thomson's tube and its crossed fields.

concepts.name: Millikan's oil drop measures the electron's charge, $q = m_{\text{drop}}\kg\kd/\kV$
concepts.why: The charge of the electron was measured directly by holding a drop of oil still. When the weight of a charged drop is balanced by the electric force between two plates, its charge follows from its mass, the plate separation and the voltage. Millikan found that every charge is a multiple of one basic charge, which is the quantization of charge the reader met in Chapter 18, now seen in a single drop.
concepts.evidence: The book writes the balance $m_{\text{drop}}g = q_eE$, uses $E = V/d$ to obtain $q = m_{\text{drop}}gd/V$, and says that by 1913 Millikan had measured the charge to an accuracy of 1 percent and observed that all charges were multiples of the basic electron charge. Figure 30.9 draws the apparatus, and the section's second test-prep item asks which fields hold drops of equal mass motionless.

concepts.name: The mass of the electron, $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg
concepts.why: With the charge from Millikan and the ratio from Thomson, the mass of the electron is one division away. It is an incredibly small mass, the smallest of any particle that has mass, and the proton, about 1836 times heavier, carries nearly all the mass of a hydrogen atom. The reader should be able to do the division and to say what it means: the electron is a tiny fraction of the atom's mass.
concepts.evidence: The book divides $-1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C by $-1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg to obtain $m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, gives the proton's mass as $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, and asks in a conceptual question which two pieces of evidence allowed the first calculation of the electron's mass.

concepts.name: All electrons are identical
concepts.why: The charge and mass of the electron are not averages over many electrons; every electron has exactly the same values. This is a new kind of fact about nature, one that has no counterpart among the grains of sand or the planets of everyday physics, and it is the ground on which the exclusion principle of 30.9 will stand.
concepts.evidence: The book says that all electrons are identical to one another, that the charge and mass of electrons are not average values but unique values that all electrons have, and that the same is true of other fundamental entities, so that all protons are identical to one another. Thomson always found the same properties for electrons freed from different gases.

concepts.name: Rutherford scattering reveals a tiny, massive nucleus
concepts.why: Rutherford's gold foil experiment is the reason we picture the atom as mostly empty. Most alpha particles went straight through the foil, but a few came almost straight back, which only a very small, very massive, positively charged center could do. The reader should be able to argue from the pattern of scattering to the size and mass of the nucleus, about $10^{-15}$ m across, 100,000 times smaller than the atom.
concepts.evidence: The book says that alpha particles occasionally were scattered to large angles, some even back in the direction from which they came, that about once in 8000 times an alpha hits a nucleus head-on, and that the size of the nucleus was determined to be about $10^{-15}$ m, implying a density on the order of $10^{15}$ g/cm³. Figures 30.10 and 30.11 draw the experiment and the foil.

concepts.name: The planetary model of the atom
concepts.why: Rutherford's result needs a picture, and the planetary model is the one the rest of the chapter works with. Low-mass electrons orbit a small, massive nucleus at distances large compared with its size, held by the Coulomb force as the planets are held by gravity. Bohr builds his theory on this picture in 30.3, and 30.6 shows where it must give way.
concepts.evidence: The book says that Rutherford proposed the planetary model of the atom, which pictures low-mass electrons orbiting a large-mass nucleus with mostly vacuum inside the atom, and that in the atom the attractive Coulomb force is analogous to gravitation in the planetary system. Figure 30.12 draws the model.

concepts.name: Atomic spectra are discrete
concepts.why: An atom does not glow in every color; it emits and absorbs only certain wavelengths, and each element has its own set. This is the mystery Bohr solved, and the reader should hold it clearly before the solution: the lines are the atom's fingerprint, and their discreteness says that the atom's energies are quantized.
concepts.evidence: The book says that atomic and molecular emission and absorption spectra have been known for over a century to be discrete, that the line spectrum for each element is unique, and that the discrete lines imply quantized energy states for the atoms that produce them. Figure 30.14 shows the line spectrum of iron, and two conceptual questions ask what discrete means and why cold hydrogen absorbs only the Lyman series.

concepts.name: Hydrogen's wavelengths, $1/\klam = R(1/n_{\text{f}}^2 - 1/n_{\text{i}}^2)$
concepts.why: Hydrogen, with its single electron, has the simplest spectrum, and one formula gives every line of it. Each series ends on one level, $n_{\text{f}} = 1$ for the Lyman series in the ultraviolet, 2 for the Balmer series that reaches into the visible, 3 for the Paschen series in the infrared, and the Rydberg constant sets the scale. What was first a recipe to fit data is later derived from Bohr's theory, and the reader should be able to use it either way.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$ with $R = 1.097 \times 10^{7}$ m⁻¹, names the series, and in Example 30.1 finds the second Balmer line at 486 nm. It then shows that $(13.6\ \text{eV})/hc$ equals $R$, so that Bohr's assumptions derive the formula first proposed by Balmer. Several problems ask for lines in each series and whether the series overlap.

concepts.name: A photon carries the energy between two orbits, $\kdE = hf = \kEini - \kEfin$
concepts.why: Bohr's first proposal is that the orbits are quantized and that an electron moves between them by absorbing or emitting a photon. The photon's energy is exactly the difference between the two orbital energies, so a quantized set of orbits gives a quantized set of photons, which is a discrete spectrum. This one equation joins the atom's structure to the light it gives off.
concepts.evidence: The book states that each orbit has a different energy, that electrons move to a higher orbit by absorbing energy and drop to a lower orbit by emitting energy, and writes $\Delta E = hf = E_i - E_f$ for the photon. Figure 30.16 draws the quantized orbits, and the section's first test-prep item asks for the levels of an atom that can emit only photons of $2E$, $3E$ and $5E$.

concepts.name: Read and draw an energy-level diagram
concepts.why: An energy-level diagram plots the allowed energies of a system vertically, the ground state at the bottom, and draws each transition as an arrow between two levels. It is how atomic, molecular and nuclear physics show what a system can do at a glance, and every later section of this chapter, from the x rays of 30.4 to the laser of 30.5, is read from one.
concepts.evidence: The book says that an energy-level diagram is a convenient way to display energy states, with energy plotted vertically, the lowest or ground state at the bottom and excited states above. Figure 30.17 shows a transition from $E_4$ to $E_2$, and Figure 30.19 shows hydrogen's levels with the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen transitions.

concepts.name: Bohr's quantized angular momentum, $\kL = m_{\text{e}}\kv\krn = nh/2\pi$
concepts.why: To compute the energies, Bohr assumed that the angular momentum of an electron in its orbit can take only whole multiples of $h/2\pi$. At the time he did not know why, and 30.6 gives the reason, but with this one rule and the physics of circular motion he could calculate the whole spectrum of hydrogen, something no one had done.
concepts.evidence: The book states that Bohr proposed that the angular momentum $L$ of an electron in its orbit is quantized, gives $L = m_evr_n = nh/2\pi$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, and notes that for a small object at radius $r$, $L = mvr$. A conceptual question asks how Bohr's rule differs from the actual rule.

concepts.name: The radii of the allowed orbits, $\krn = (n^2/Z)\kaB$
concepts.why: Setting the Coulomb force equal to the centripetal force, and taking the speed from the quantized angular momentum, gives the radius of every allowed orbit of a hydrogen-like atom. The radii grow as $n^2$, and the smallest, the Bohr radius of 0.529 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, is the measured size of hydrogen, which is a striking success for a theory built from so little.
concepts.evidence: The book equates $kZq_e^2/r_n^2$ with $m_ev^2/r_n$, obtains $r_n = (n^2/Z)a_B$ with $a_B = h^2/4\pi^2m_ekq_e^2 = 0.529 \times 10^{-10}$ m, and says it is impressive that the formula gives the correct size of hydrogen. Figure 30.18 draws the first four orbits, and problems ask for the radius of the $n = 2$ state and of a muon's orbit in uranium.

concepts.name: The energies of hydrogen-like atoms, $\kEn = -(Z^2/n^2)\kEobohr$
concepts.why: The orbital energy is the sum of the electron's kinetic energy and its negative electric potential energy, and with Bohr's radii it comes out as $-13.6$ eV divided by $n^2$ for hydrogen. The energies are negative because the electron is bound, they crowd together toward zero as $n$ grows, and their differences reproduce every line of the spectrum. The same formula, with $Z^2$, serves any atom stripped to one electron.
concepts.evidence: The book writes $E_n = \text{KE} + \text{PE}$, substitutes the radius and speed to obtain $E_n = -(Z^2/n^2)E_0$ with $E_0 = 13.6$ eV, and gives $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$ for hydrogen. Figure 30.19 is the energy-level diagram it produces, and a conceptual question asks how the energies and radii of a hydrogen-like atom are related to those in hydrogen.

concepts.name: Find the energy needed to ionize an atom from a given level
concepts.why: An electron at zero energy is free, so the energy needed to ionize an atom from level $n$ is just the size of $E_n$. This is the skill the section's problems use most: 13.6 eV from the ground state of hydrogen, much less from an excited state, and any energy beyond that goes into the freed electron's kinetic energy.
concepts.evidence: The book says that 13.6 eV is needed to ionize hydrogen, an experimentally verified number, and that giving 15.0 eV to an electron in the ground state strips it from the atom and leaves it with 1.4 eV of kinetic energy. Problems ask for the energy to ionize hydrogen from $n = 4$ and a Be³⁺ ion from an excited state, and a test-prep item asks for the photon that ionizes and leaves the electron $2E_0$.

concepts.name: The triumphs and limits of Bohr's theory
concepts.why: Bohr explained the spectrum and the size of hydrogen and showed that orbital energies and angular momentum are quantized, but his orbits are semiclassical, quantized yet imagined as circles. The theory cannot treat an atom with two electrons and cannot explain doublets, and the reader should carry both halves forward, since 30.6 to 30.9 replace the orbits with clouds of probability while keeping the quantization.
concepts.evidence: The book lists the triumphs, that Bohr explained the spectrum of hydrogen, correctly calculated the size of the atom and showed why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus, and the limits, that the theory cannot be applied to multielectron atoms, that there are no well-defined orbits but clouds of probability, and that it did not explain doublets.

concepts.name: An x-ray tube makes bremsstrahlung and characteristic x rays
concepts.why: An x-ray tube produces two kinds of radiation at once, and its spectrum shows both. Electrons slowing in the anode give a broad, smooth curve of braking radiation, and electrons that knock out inner-shell electrons give sharp peaks characteristic of the anode material. The reader should be able to point to each part of the spectrum and say where it came from.
concepts.evidence: The book says that there are two processes by which x rays are produced in the anode, the deceleration of electrons, which gives bremsstrahlung, and an atomic process that produces characteristic x rays. Figure 30.20 shows a broad curve of bremsstrahlung radiation with characteristic peaks on it.

concepts.name: The highest x-ray energy, $\kEmax = hf_{\text{max}} = \kqe\kV$
concepts.why: The most energetic x ray a tube can make is the one for which an electron's whole kinetic energy becomes a single photon. Since the electron gained that energy from the accelerating voltage, the maximum photon energy in electron volts is the voltage in volts, so a 100-kV tube makes photons of at most 100 keV. This conservation of energy sets the sharp end of the spectrum.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the accelerating voltage and the maximum x-ray energy are related by conservation of energy, writes $E_{\text{max}} = hf_{\text{max}} = q_eV$, and gives the example of a 100-kV voltage. Two keyed problems ask for the shortest wavelength and the most energetic photon from tubes at 50.0 kV and 100 kV.

concepts.name: Estimate a characteristic x-ray energy from hydrogen-like levels
concepts.why: A characteristic x ray is emitted when an inner-shell vacancy is filled, and it is labeled by the shell with the vacancy and the shell the electron came from: $K_\alpha$ for $n = 2$ to $n = 1$, $K_\beta$ for $n = 3$ to $n = 1$. Inner electrons feel nearly the whole nucleus, so their energies are close to hydrogen-like with an effective charge of $Z - 1$, and the reader can estimate an element's x rays with 30.3's formula.
concepts.evidence: Example 30.3 calculates the $K_\alpha$ energy of tungsten with an effective charge of 73, finding $E_1 = -72.5$ keV, $E_2 = -18.1$ keV and an x ray of 54.4 keV, and notes that the energies grow approximately as $Z^2$. Figure 30.21 labels the transitions, and a keyed problem asks for the $K_\alpha$ and $K_\beta$ energies of copper.

concepts.name: X-ray images are shadows, and CT builds them in three dimensions
concepts.why: Because x-ray photons are energetic, they pass through materials that are opaque to visible light, and denser material stops more of them, leaving a darker shadow. That is why x rays show bones, fillings and the contents of luggage, and why a CT scanner, which passes x rays through a slice of the body from many directions, can build a detailed image of what a single shadow would hide.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the most common x-ray images are simple shadows, that the denser the material, the fewer x-ray photons get through and the darker the shadow, and that a CT scanner passes x rays through a narrow slice over a range of directions and analyzes the relative absorption by computer. Figures 30.22 to 30.26 show the images and the scanner.

concepts.name: X-ray diffraction reveals the arrangement of atoms
concepts.why: An x ray's wavelength is about the size of an atom, so while x rays cast sharp shadows of teeth they diffract from the regular rows of atoms in a crystal. The pattern that results can be analyzed to find where the atoms are, which is how the double helix of DNA was found and how von Laue proved that x rays are waves.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the 54.4-keV $K_\alpha$ x ray has a wavelength of 0.0228 nm, that atoms are on the order of 0.1 nm in size, and that x-ray diffraction involves the diffraction and interference of x rays to produce patterns that can be analyzed for information about the structures that scattered them. Figure 30.27 shows the pattern from a protein crystal.

concepts.name: Color and transparency come from atomic energy levels
concepts.why: The color of a material is set by which photon energies its atoms can absorb. A tomato is red because its pigment has levels for every visible photon energy except red, and air is transparent because visible photons find almost no levels to excite in its molecules. The reader should be able to explain a color with an energy-level diagram rather than with the word pigment.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the color of a material is due to the ability of its atoms to absorb certain wavelengths while reflecting or reemitting others, gives the tomato and air as examples, and a test-prep item asks why the leaves of a tree are green.

concepts.name: Fluorescence, de-excitation in smaller steps
concepts.why: An atom excited several steps up by an ultraviolet photon may come down in one step or in several, and when it comes down in smaller steps it emits photons of lower energy, some of them visible. That is fluorescence: black lights, glowing scorpions and minerals, brighter laundry and the fluorescent tube all work this way, and the reader should be able to draw the steps on an energy-level diagram.
concepts.evidence: The book defines fluorescence as any process in which an atom or molecule, excited by a photon of a given energy, de-excites by emission of a lower-energy photon, and describes atomic excitation and de-excitation. Figure 30.29 shows a scorpion glowing under an ultraviolet lamp, and three test-prep items ask about fluorescence.

concepts.name: Metastable states and phosphorescence
concepts.why: Most excited states decay in about $10^{-8}$ s, but some live for milliseconds to hours, and these are called metastable. Their slow decay is phosphorescence, the glow of a luminous dial, and the energy frozen into a fired ceramic lets its age be read by thermoluminescence. The metastable state is also the heart of every laser.
concepts.evidence: The book says that spontaneous de-excitation has a very short mean lifetime of typically about $10^{-8}$ s, that some levels have significantly longer lifetimes and are said to be metastable, and that phosphorescence is the de-excitation of a metastable state. Figure 30.33 shows a ceramic dated by thermoluminescence.

concepts.name: Population inversion
concepts.why: When energy is pumped into many atoms with a metastable level, most fall back quickly but those in the metastable state linger, and a majority of atoms can end up there. This condition, a population inversion, is what a laser needs, because a photon is as likely to be absorbed by an atom below as to stimulate one above, so the atoms above must outnumber those below.
concepts.evidence: The book says that it is possible to get a majority of the atoms into the metastable state, a condition called a population inversion, and that the probability of absorption of a photon is the same as the probability of stimulated emission, so a majority of atoms must be in the metastable state. Figure 30.34 draws the levels before and after pumping.

concepts.name: Stimulated emission
concepts.why: A photon passing an atom in an excited state can trigger it to emit a second photon with the same energy, the same phase, the same polarization and the same direction. One photon becomes two, two become four, and the light builds up in step. Einstein saw in 1917 that this must happen, decades before anyone could build the device that uses it.
concepts.evidence: The book defines stimulated emission as the emission of photons of a given frequency triggered by photons of the same frequency, says that the emitted and triggering photons are always in phase, have the same polarization and travel in the same direction, and credits Einstein. Figure 30.35 draws the cascade.

concepts.name: The laser, light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation
concepts.why: A laser puts population inversion and stimulated emission together between two mirrors, so that the light passes back and forth through the lasing material many times and a small fraction escapes through the partly silvered end. Its output is a single wavelength and coherent, and that is why it can be focused to a small spot, read a disc, weld a retina or record a hologram.
concepts.evidence: The book says that lasers produce single-wavelength electromagnetic radiation that is also very coherent, explains the mirrors in Figure 30.36, and draws the helium and neon levels of the common red laser in Figure 30.37, whose 1.96-eV photons have a wavelength of 633 nm. Conceptual questions ask about lasers for discs and about holograms.

concepts.name: Find the wavelength of a photon from the spacing of two levels
concepts.why: Every problem of this section asks the same thing of an energy-level diagram: take the difference between two levels in electron volts and turn it into a wavelength. With $hc = 1240$ eV·nm the step is one division, and it tells the reader whether a laser line or a pumping photon is infrared, visible or ultraviolet.
concepts.evidence: The keyed problems find the 633-nm helium-neon line as $(1240\ \text{eV·nm})/(1.96\ \text{eV})$, the 693-nm ruby line from the chromium levels and the 1.06-μm neodymium line from a 1.17-eV transition, and two integrated problems ask for the photon energies of an excimer laser and a surgical laser.

concepts.name: Holography records a three-dimensional image by interference
concepts.why: A hologram is made with coherent laser light split into two beams, one lighting the object and one falling directly on the film, and the film records the interference of the two. Lit again by the same kind of laser, the film acts like a set of diffraction gratings and rebuilds the light from the object, so the image changes with the viewpoint just as the object would.
concepts.evidence: The book says that holography uses light interference or wave optics, whereas normal photography uses geometric optics, that light scattered from the object interferes with the reference beam, and that moving your eye to various places in the pattern gives you different perspectives. Figures 30.42 and 30.43 draw the recording and the viewing, and a conceptual question asks how to tell that a hologram is truly three-dimensional.

concepts.name: An allowed orbit holds a whole number of wavelengths, $n\klamorb = 2\pi\krn$
concepts.why: An electron bound to an atom has a wavelength, and in a circular orbit that wave must meet itself crest to crest, like a standing wave on a string bent into a ring. Only orbits whose circumference is a whole number of wavelengths allow this constructive interference, so only certain orbits exist. The quantization Bohr had to assume is a consequence of the wave nature of matter.
concepts.evidence: The book gives the condition for constructive interference and an allowed orbit as $n\lambda_n = 2\pi r_n$, compares it with waves on a string, and draws an orbit that fits and one that does not in Figure 30.44. Figure 30.45 shows three and four wavelengths around the third and fourth orbits, and a test-prep item asks which circumferences are disallowed.

concepts.name: The wave condition gives Bohr's rule, $\kL = m_{\text{e}}\kv\krn = nh/2\pi$
concepts.why: Putting the de Broglie wavelength into the standing-wave condition turns it into exactly the quantization of angular momentum that Bohr assumed. This is the answer to the question Bohr could not answer, why angular momentum is quantized, and it also says why the electron cannot spiral into the nucleus: there is a lowest orbit where the wave can fit.
concepts.evidence: The book substitutes $\lambda = h/m_ev$ into $n\lambda_n = 2\pi r_n$, rearranges to $L = m_evr_n = nh/2\pi$, and says that this is what Bohr was forced to hypothesize and that we now realize it is the condition for constructive interference. The boxed note says that the wave nature of matter is what prevents matter from collapsing and gives atoms their sizes.

concepts.name: Orbits give way to clouds of probability
concepts.why: Because the electron is a wave, it has no well-defined orbit. Each measurement finds it at a definite place, but repeated measurements build up a cloud of probability, densest near the Bohr radius for the ground state of hydrogen and very thin far from the nucleus. This picture replaces Bohr's circles from here to the end of the chapter.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the idea of well-defined orbits gives way to a model in which there is a cloud of probability, consistent with Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, and that repeated measurements reveal a cloud with each speck the location determined by a single measurement. Figure 30.46 shows the cloud for the ground state of hydrogen.

concepts.name: The Zeeman effect, spectral lines split by a magnetic field
concepts.why: Placed in a magnetic field, a spectral line splits into three, five or more lines, and the spacing grows in proportion to the field. That tells us that an orbit's quantized energy is changed by the field, so each orbit has several discrete energies instead of one, and it is the clue that led to the next two kinds of quantization.
concepts.evidence: The book defines the Zeeman effect as spectral lines being split into two or more separate lines by an external magnetic field, says that the amount the split lines are separated is proportional to the applied field strength, and shows the splitting at two field strengths in Figure 30.47. The section's conceptual question asks what the effect is and what quantization it revealed.

concepts.name: An orbiting electron is a current loop with its own magnetic field
concepts.why: In Bohr's picture the orbiting electron is a small current loop, and a current loop makes a magnetic field along its axis, the same line as its orbital angular momentum. An external field exerts a torque on the loop, so an orbit tilted to the field has a different energy from one aligned with it. This is why a magnetic field can change the energy of an orbit at all.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the circular orbit forms a current loop which creates a magnetic field of its own, $B_{\text{orb}}$, that $B_{\text{orb}}$ and the orbital angular momentum are along the same line, and that the external and orbital fields interact through a torque, so that orbits at different angles to the field have different energies. Figure 30.48 draws the loop.

concepts.name: Space quantization, only certain directions of angular momentum
concepts.why: Since the Zeeman lines are discrete, the energies of the tilted orbits are discrete, and so only certain angles are allowed between the orbital angular momentum and the field. The direction of angular momentum is quantized as well as its magnitude, which is totally unexpected: the Moon's orbit can point any way at all.
concepts.evidence: The book says that only certain angles are allowed between the orbital angular momentum and the external field, that the direction of the orbital angular momentum is also quantized, and that this is called space quantization. Figure 30.49 draws the allowed directions.

concepts.name: Electron spin and fine structure
concepts.why: Even with no field, close examination shows that spectral lines are doublets. The cause is that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum, its spin, and with it an intrinsic magnetic field, which can point at only one of two angles to another field, spin up or spin down. The two directions have different energies, and the line splits in two.
concepts.evidence: The book says that spectral lines are closely spaced doublets, a characteristic called fine structure, that Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck argued in 1925 that electrons have an intrinsic spin with an intrinsic magnetic field, and that the spin's direction can be at only one of two angles relative to a magnetic field. Figures 30.50 and 30.51 show the doublets and the two directions.

concepts.name: Quantum numbers, and the principal quantum number $n$
concepts.why: The values of quantized quantities are labeled by quantum numbers, and the rules for them govern atoms, chemistry and much more. The first is the principal quantum number $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, which labels the basic states of a system and sets the energy of the hydrogen atom and its orbital radii.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the values of quantized entities are expressed in terms of quantum numbers, defines $n$ as the principal quantum number that labels the basic states of a system, and notes that the energy of the hydrogen atom can be expressed as a function of $n$. Four conceptual questions ask the reader to define the quantum numbers and state their allowed values.

concepts.name: The magnitude of angular momentum, $\kL = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,h/2\pi$
concepts.why: Quantum mechanics replaces Bohr's rule with the magnitude $\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,h/2\pi$, where the angular momentum quantum number $l$ runs from 0 to $n - 1$. For the ground state $l$ must be zero, so the ground state of hydrogen has no angular momentum at all, which is one more sign that the circular orbit is not the right picture.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,h/2\pi$ with $l = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$, notes that for $n = 1$ the ground-state angular momentum is zero, not $h/2\pi$ as Bohr proposed, and works out $L = 2.58 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s for $l = 2$. Keyed problems ask for the angular momentum of an $l = 1$ electron and compare it with Bohr's value.

concepts.name: The allowed components, $\kLz = m_l h/2\pi$
concepts.why: The direction of angular momentum is quantized because its component along the field, the $z$-axis, can take only the values $m_l h/2\pi$, with $m_l$ running from $-l$ to $l$ in steps of one. Each value of $m_l$ has a different energy in a magnetic field, which is the Zeeman splitting of 30.7 written as a rule.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $L_z = m_lh/2\pi$ with $m_l = -l, -l + 1, \ldots, l$, lists the five values for $l = 2$, and says that each $m_l$ corresponds to a different energy in the presence of a magnetic field. Figure 30.52 draws the three components for $l = 1$, and keyed problems ask for the allowed values of $m_l$ and $l$.

concepts.name: Find the angles angular momentum can make with the $z$-axis
concepts.why: Since $\kLz$ is one side of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $\kL$, the allowed angles follow from $\cos\theta = \kLz/\kL$. The vectors lie on cones about the axis, and as $l$ grows the smallest angle approaches zero and the allowed angles crowd together, which is how the correspondence principle is satisfied.
concepts.evidence: Example 30.4 finds the angles 45.0°, 90.0° and 135.0° for $l = 1$ from $\cos\theta = L_z/L$ and discusses the limit of large $l$. A keyed problem asks for the angles the electron's spin can make with the $z$-axis, 54.7° and 125.3°.

concepts.name: Spin, $\kSspin = \sqrt{s(s+1)}\,h/2\pi$ and $\kSz = m_s h/2\pi$
concepts.why: The electron's spin is quantized in magnitude and in direction in the same way as its orbital angular momentum, but with one fixed value, $s = 1/2$. Its component along the $z$-axis can be only $+1/2$ or $-1/2$ times $h/2\pi$, spin up or spin down. With this fourth quantum number, the state of an electron in an atom is fully given by $(n, l, m_l, m_s)$.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $S = \sqrt{s(s+1)}\,h/2\pi$ with $s = 1/2$ for electrons and $S_z = m_sh/2\pi$ with $m_s = \pm 1/2$, and Table 30.1 summarizes the atomic quantum numbers and their allowed values. Keyed problems ask for the spin angular momentum and its ratio to an orbital one.

concepts.name: State the allowed sets of quantum numbers $(n, l, m_l, m_s)$
concepts.why: The four rules chain together: $n$ is a positive integer, $l$ runs from 0 to $n - 1$, $m_l$ from $-l$ to $l$, and $m_s$ is $\pm 1/2$. The reader who can list the allowed sets for a given $n$, and say which rule a forbidden set breaks, has what 30.9 needs to count the electrons in a shell.
concepts.evidence: Table 30.1 lists the atomic quantum numbers with their allowed values, and the section's conceptual questions and keyed problems ask for the possible values of $l$ given $n = 5$ and $m_l = 3$ and the possible values of $m_l$ for $n = 4$.

concepts.name: The Pauli exclusion principle
concepts.why: No two electrons can have the same set of quantum numbers; no two electrons can be in the same state. This single rule is why atoms are not all crowded into their ground states, why only two electrons fit in the $n = 1$ level, and, through the shells it forces, why the elements have the chemistry they have.
concepts.evidence: The book states in a boxed note that no two electrons can have the same set of quantum numbers, that is, no two electrons can be in the same state, says that it applies to any identical particles with half-integral spin, and draws allowed and forbidden arrangements in the $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ levels in Figure 30.55.

concepts.name: Shells, subshells and spectroscopic notation
concepts.why: Each value of $n$ is a shell and each value of $l$ within it a subshell, written with a letter: $s$, $p$, $d$, $f$ for $l = 0, 1, 2, 3$. Spectroscopic notation such as $2p^3$ gives the shell, the subshell and the number of electrons in it, and the reader should be able to read and write it and say when a notation breaks a rule.
concepts.evidence: The book says that each value of the principal quantum number corresponds to an atomic shell and each value of $l$ to a subshell, gives the symbols in Table 30.2, and explains the notation $2p^3$ in Figure 30.56. Conceptual questions and keyed problems ask which notations are not allowed and which rule each violates.

concepts.name: A subshell holds at most $2(2l+1)$ electrons
concepts.why: Once $l$ is known there are $2l + 1$ values of $m_l$, each with two values of $m_s$, so a subshell can hold at most $2(2l + 1)$ electrons: 2 in an $s$ subshell, 6 in a $p$, 10 in a $d$. Counting from the rules is what turns the exclusion principle into numbers.
concepts.evidence: The book derives the maximum number of electrons in a subshell as $2(2l+1)$, uses it for the $2s$ and $2p$ subshells of Example 30.5's table, and in Example 30.6 finds 2, 6 and 10 for the $3s$, $3p$ and $3d$ subshells.

concepts.name: A shell holds at most $2n^2$ electrons
concepts.why: Adding the subshells of a shell gives at most $2n^2$ electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, 18 in the third, 32 in the fourth. These are the lengths the periods of the periodic table are built from.
concepts.evidence: The book says that some algebra shows that the maximum number of electrons that can be in a shell is $2n^2$, and Example 30.6 verifies that the three subshells of $n = 3$ hold 18. A keyed problem asks how many electrons can be in the $n = 4$ shell and in each of its subshells.

concepts.name: Shell filling explains the periodic table
concepts.why: As electrons are added from hydrogen to calcium, the lowest shells and subshells fill first, with exceptions such as potassium whose $4s$ fills before $3d$. The outermost electrons decide the chemistry: a filled outer subshell makes a noble gas, one vacancy a halogen, one extra $s$ electron an alkali metal. Mendeleev's groups have their explanation in the substructure of the atom.
concepts.evidence: Table 30.3 gives the configurations of the first twenty elements, and the book says that the number of electrons in the outermost subshell determines the atom's chemical properties, describing the noble gases of Group 18, the halogens of Group 17 and the alkali metals of Group 1. Figure 30.58 is the periodic table.
